text.hook:
"RVO is guaranteed since C++17."
Half true, and interviewers ask about the other half.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Guaranteed vs optional elision
2. What every return statement costs
3. How NRVO works in the ABI
4. Implicit move, standard by standard
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: RVO, NRVO and implicit move: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: Two very different things share one name

cards.label: Guaranteed (C++17)
cards.text: A **prvalue** initializes its final object directly. No copy or move constructor needed, not even an accessible one.

cards.label: Permitted (optional)
cards.text: **NRVO** for a named local. The compiler *may* skip the move. The constructor must still be usable.

slides.takeaway: Returning a local by value: NRVO (0 ops), else implicit move (1 move), else copy (only if no move constructor is declared).

slides.title: What each `return` really costs
slides.takeaway: `return local.member;` copies too: a member is not implicitly movable. Here `std::move` is correct.

slides.title: How NRVO actually works
steps: the caller reserves space for the result and passes its address as a hidden argument
`return T{...};` runs the constructor directly at that address (RVO)
`T t; return t;` places `t` itself at that address from the start (NRVO)
two candidates, or a parameter (caller-owned storage): no NRVO, implicit move

slides.title: Elision only happens at initialization

cards.label: `a = make();`
cards.text: A temporary is materialized, move-assigned into `a`, then destroyed: `ctor move-assign dtor`.

slides.takeaway: Assigning a fresh object into a container throws away its old capacity. In hot loops, refill an existing object instead.

slides.title: `return x;` moves: what changed, standard by standard
rows: `x` is a local or a by-value parameter
the returned name simply *is* an xvalue
slides.takeaway: Never covered: members, globals, statics. Structured bindings: compilers differ. Need a move? Write `std::move`.

slides.lead: A copy or move constructor that logs or counts may simply never run. Never put essential work (registration, ref counting) only there.

items.truth: Elision from a **prvalue** is guaranteed. NRVO (`return local;`) is still optional.

items.myth: "If NRVO does not happen, the object is copied."
items.truth: It is moved (implicit move). Copied only if no move constructor is declared.

items.myth: "A deleted move constructor makes `return local;` fall back to copy."
items.truth: The deleted move is selected: ill-formed. Rejected by GCC in C++20 and by Clang in every mode (GCC 11 in C++17 mode still accepts it).
Its storage belongs to the caller's argument. It is moved, never elided.
A conditional of two lvalues is an lvalue: it copies. Use `if (cond) return a; return b;`.
Since C++17 it can only disable NRVO. Prvalue elision has nothing to elide.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Four constructor calls in the source.
How many actually run in C++17?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Count the objects, not the parentheses.

slides.title: C++17. Which constructors run?

slides.verdict_sub: One object, built directly in `x` (guaranteed since C++17)
bullets: Each `T(...)` around a prvalue of type `T` is a prvalue with the **same result object**.
No copy, no move: it compiles even with deleted copy and move constructors.
C++14 with `-fno-elide-constructors` prints a chain of moves instead.

slides.title: C++17 with `-fno-elide-constructors`

columns.label: prvalue (RVO)
named (NRVO)

slides.takeaway: A prvalue is a recipe, not a temporary: there is nothing to elide. Only NRVO can be switched off.

text.hook:
"Add std::move to make sure it moves."
A code review comment you have probably seen.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: What does the program print, and which line would you flag in review?

slides.title:
"Make sure it moves."
Which special members run?

slides.verdict_sub: Output `ctor move dtor dtor`. GCC `-Wall`: "moving a local object in a return statement prevents copy elision"
bullets: `std::move(result)` is a function call expression, **not the name of a local**.
So NRVO is not allowed: the result is move-constructed.
`result` is then destroyed at the end of `build()`: one extra move, one extra destructor.
`return result;` gives `ctor dtor` (NRVO), or at worst one implicit move.

slides.title: Return locals by name
slides.tip: `std::move` in a return *is* right for members and sub-objects: `return std::move(p.first);`
slides.takeaway: `return local;` and `return param;` never need `std::move`. Adding it can only add a move.

text.hook:
Copy constructor: deleted. Move constructor: deleted.
"The compiler elides the copy anyway."
So both functions compile?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This is how factories return types that hold a std::mutex or a std::atomic.

slides.title: C++17. Which function compiles?

slides.verdict_sub: Prvalue return: yes. Named return: never.
bullets: `return NM{1};` is a prvalue: it initializes the caller's object directly. No constructor needed.
`return x;` relies on NRVO, which is optional. The code must be valid without it: "use of deleted function".
In C++14 `f1` fails too. Guaranteed elision is C++17.

slides.title: Created by a factory, never relocated
slides.code:
NM a = f1();             // OK (C++17)
std::atomic<int> x = 5;  // OK (C++17)
a = f1();   // error: no operator=
slides.tip: Same idea: a factory returning `std::lock_guard`. All of these fail in C++14.
slides.takeaway: Non-movable types are returnable as prvalues only. They cannot live in a `std::vector` that grows.

text.hook:
"Always take a std::string by const&. It avoids copies."
This constructor stores its argument.
How many copies happen?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Three callers: an lvalue, a std::move and a temporary.

slides.title: How many `copy` lines?

slides.verdict_sub: `const&` forces a copy into the member, even from a temporary
bullets: `id_(id)`: `id` is a const lvalue, so the member is always copy-constructed.
`std::move(t)` and `Str{}` bind to `const&` and lose their rvalue-ness.
For a **stored** parameter, the `const&` reflex wastes every temporary.
slides.wrong: "1: only the lvalue copies, rvalues get moved"

slides.title: Sink by value, then move
slides.code:
Order(Str id) : id_(std::move(id)) {}

Order a(s);             // copy move
Order b(std::move(t));  // move move
Order c(Str{});         // move
slides.tip: A `const&` + `&&` overload pair saves one move, but needs 2^N overloads for N parameters.
slides.takeaway: Stored parameter: by value + `std::move`. Read-only parameter: `const&` or a view.
